claims.claim: Body temperature reflects the balance between heat produced and heat lost; heat is produced in the body during muscle movement and the normal physical and chemical processes of metabolism, and temperature is one of the four main measurements routinely monitored along with heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure.

The average normal body temperature is generally accepted as 98.6F (37C), and normal adult body temperature can range roughly from 97F (36.1C) to 99F (37.2C); normal temperature varies by person, age, activity, and time of day.

Temperature is measured at several sites — oral (under the tongue, the most common route), rectal (the most accurate and the standard for infants, also the most invasive), axillary (armpit, minimally invasive and often used for young children, reading about 1F lower than oral), tympanic (probe in the ear), and temporal (infrared scan across the forehead) — and readings differ slightly by site.
A fever is a body temperature that is higher than normal; it is not a disease — it is usually a sign that the body is trying to fight an illness or infection, and infections cause most fevers.
Hypothermia is a low body temperature, usually below 95F (35C), and is a danger commonly linked to prolonged cold exposure.

Body temperature changes with illness (infection commonly raises it), exercise (working muscles produce heat), the environment (cold air, wind, or wet clothing pull heat out; prolonged exposure can drive temperature down), and time of day (lowest in the early morning, higher later in the day).
A single temperature reading is one clue that gains meaning only in context — the site, the time of day, recent activity, and the rest of the assessment — not a verdict by itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What threshold counts as a fever
positions: MedlinePlus Vital Signs topic: a body temperature higher than normal (over 98.6F / 37C) is called a fever.
MedlinePlus Body temperature norms: a temperature over 100.4F (38C) most often means a fever caused by an infection or illness.
OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: fever onset is described at about 100F (37.8C) and 100.4F (38C) is a common clinical reference point.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines fever simply as temperature above the normal range, presents 100.4F (38C) as the commonly cited fever threshold (attributed to MedlinePlus), and notes that exact thresholds vary by source, age, and measurement site. No single threshold is asserted as universal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Normal range differs by measurement site
positions: OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills: axillary readings run about 1F (0.6C) lower than oral; rectal readings run about 0.5F to 1F (0.3-0.6C) higher than oral; tympanic runs slightly higher than oral.
MedlinePlus temperature measurement: ear thermometers are common but some users report less accuracy than probe thermometers; forehead thermometers are more accurate than ear thermometers.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states site differences factually (axillary about 1F lower, rectal about 0.5-1F higher) and teaches that the site must be part of interpreting any reading, without inventing a single universal number.
